Learn how to analyse bulk RNA-Seq data, from experimental design and raw sequencing data through quality control, alignment, gene-expression quantification, differential expression, visualisation, and functional analysis.

Learn how to use Bayesian modelling and R-INLA to analyse hierarchical, spatial, temporal, and other complex ecological datasets.

Ecological data frequently contain hierarchical structure, spatial and temporal dependence, repeated observations, missing values, and multiple sources of uncertainty. Bayesian modelling provides a powerful framework for handling these complexities, while INLA offers an efficient approach for fitting many sophisticated Bayesian models without the computational demands of conventional MCMC methods. This course provides practical, hands-on training in Bayesian inference and R-INLA, with methods directly applicable to ecological and environmental research.

These approaches have particularly strong applications in molecular ecology, conservation genetics, evolutionary ecology, landscape genetics, population connectivity, local adaptation, and the study of demographic history.

Path Analysis, Structural Equations and Causal Inference for Biologists (PSCB04) ? Applications for Ecology

https://prstats.org/course/path-analysis-structural-equations-and-causal-inference-for-biologists-pscb04/

Delivered by Prof. John William (Bill) Shipley, Professor Emeritus at Universit? de Sherbrooke and a plant and statistical ecologist internationally recognised for his work on causal modelling, path analysis and structural equation modelling in ecology. Prof. Shipley is the author of Cause and Correlation in Biology and has published more than 170 peer-reviewed papers.

Learn how to use path analysis, structural equation modelling (SEM) and causal inference in R to investigate complex cause-and-effect relationships in ecological data.

Ecological systems are rarely governed by a single predictor and response. Environmental conditions, species traits, biological interactions and other ecological processes can act simultaneously through direct and indirect pathways. This course provides ecologists with a rigorous framework for formulating these relationships as causal hypotheses and testing them using the observational data typical of ecological and evolutionary research.

What you'll gain

  *   Understand causal inference using experimental and observational data
  *   Translate ecological causal hypotheses into directed acyclic graphs (DAGs)
  *   Understand d-separation and statistical conditioning
  *   Construct and test causal path models
  *   Distinguish direct and indirect causal effects
  *   Conduct piecewise structural equation modelling
  *   Use the piecewiseSEM package in R
  *   Understand equivalent models and compare competing hypotheses
  *   Use AIC for comparison of non-equivalent models
  *   Conduct covariance-based path analysis
  *   Fit structural equation models using lavaan
  *   Construct and interpret latent variables and measurement models
  *   Incorporate nested and mixed models into SEM
  *   Work with non-normal ecological data
  *   Fit and interpret multigroup models
  *   Understand causal heterogeneity
  *   Evaluate model fit and statistical power
  *   Deal with missing data and small sample sizes
  *   Report SEM results appropriately in scientific publications

Course format

  *   Dates: 19?30 October 2026
  *   Duration: 35 hours
  *   Approximately 20 hours of lectures and 15 hours of practical work
  *   Format: Live online
  *   Practical analyses conducted in R and RStudio
  *   R scripts, datasets and supporting materials provided
  *   Opportunities to work with and receive feedback on your own data
  *   All sessions recorded
  *   30 days' access to recordings
  *   30 days of post-course support
  *   Course fee: ?450

Who is this course for?

The course is particularly suitable for students and researchers working in:

  *   Ecology and evolutionary ecology
  *   Community and population ecology
  *   Plant and animal ecology
  *   Functional and trait ecology
  *   Biodiversity and conservation
  *   Environmental ecology
  *   Behavioural ecology
  *   Macroecology
  *   Ecological modelling and quantitative ecology

It is particularly useful for ecologists working with observational datasets involving multiple interacting variables, where the research question extends beyond whether variables are correlated to hypotheses about the causal processes connecting them.

Participants should have experience using R and RStudio for statistical analysis and a basic understanding of statistical inference and regression. Experience with GLMs or mixed models is useful but not required.

Why take this course?

Ecological datasets frequently contain networks of interconnected processes. For example, environmental conditions may influence species traits directly while also altering resources, competition or community composition, which subsequently affect the same ecological response. Analysing each relationship separately can make it difficult to evaluate the broader causal hypothesis.

Path analysis and SEM provide a framework for representing these hypothesised relationships explicitly and evaluating whether observed data are consistent with them. Participants will learn both piecewise SEM, which can incorporate mixed models and other model structures frequently encountered in ecological research, and covariance-based SEM, including latent-variable approaches.

Importantly, the course goes beyond simply teaching how to fit SEMs in R. It develops the underlying logic of causal inference from observational ecological data, including when causal interpretations are justified, how alternative causal structures can produce equivalent models, and how to distinguish statistical associations from defensible causal hypotheses.

Hi everyone,

Joint Species Distribution Modelling (JSDM) using HMSC: A Hierarchical Modelling Approach (JSDM01) ? Applications for Ecology

26?29 October 2026 | 22 hours | ?450 | Live Online

https://prstats.org/course/joint-species-distribution-modelling-jsdm01/

Delivered by Dr Bastien Parisy, a community ecologist and postdoctoral researcher at the University of Helsinki. His research focuses on community ecology and species interactions, particularly plant?soil microbe interactions and their responses to environmental change. His work combines field and experimental ecology with quantitative approaches including network analysis and Joint Species Distribution Models (JSDMs), particularly HMSC.

Learn how to analyse entire ecological communities using Joint Species Distribution Models in R, moving beyond traditional single-species distribution models to investigate multiple species simultaneously.

Using the Hierarchical Modelling of Species Communities (HMSC) framework, participants will learn how to relate species occurrences or abundances to environmental conditions while simultaneously incorporating species traits, phylogenetic relationships, spatial and temporal structure, and patterns of species co-occurrence within a unified hierarchical modelling framework.

What you'll gain

  *   Understand the principles of Joint Species Distribution Modelling (JSDMs)
  *   Understand the conceptual and statistical framework behind HMSC
  *   Structure multi-species ecological datasets for analysis
  *   Incorporate environmental covariates into community models
  *   Include species traits and phylogenetic information
  *   Account for spatial and temporal structure
  *   Formulate ecological hypotheses within the HMSC framework
  *   Build and fit hierarchical community models in R
  *   Understand the Bayesian and MCMC methods underlying HMSC
  *   Assess model convergence and model fit
  *   Evaluate predictive performance using cross-validation
  *   Interpret results at both species and community levels
  *   Investigate species co-occurrence and residual associations
  *   Explore environmental responses across multiple species
  *   Relate model outputs to ecological concepts such as niche theory and community assembly
  *   Produce and visualise HMSC outputs in R
  *   Report HMSC analyses appropriately in scientific manuscripts
  *   Understand extensions including spatial prediction and Hmsc-gpu

Course format

  *   Dates: 26?29 October 2026
  *   Time: 12:00?17:30 UK time each day
  *   Duration: 4 days, 5.5 hours per day (22 hours total)
  *   Format: Live online
  *   Combination of lectures and hands-on practical exercises in R
  *   Participants are encouraged to bring their own datasets for discussion
  *   Code, datasets and presentation materials provided
  *   All sessions recorded
  *   30 days' access to recordings

  *   Course fee: ?450

Who is this course for?

The course is particularly suitable for students, researchers and professionals working in:

  *   Community ecology
  *   Population and species ecology
  *   Biodiversity research
  *   Conservation biology
  *   Macroecology
  *   Spatial and temporal ecology
  *   Species distribution modelling
  *   Community assembly
  *   Species?environment relationships
  *   Species interactions and co-occurrence
  *   Quantitative ecology and ecological modelling

It is especially relevant to ecologists working with community or multi-species datasets, as well as researchers already using traditional Species Distribution Models who want to progress to modelling multiple species jointly.

Why take this course?

Traditional Species Distribution Models generally consider species individually. However, ecological communities consist of multiple species responding simultaneously to environmental conditions while differing in their traits, evolutionary relationships and spatial or temporal distributions.

Joint Species Distribution Models allow these components to be analysed together. HMSC provides a hierarchical framework for modelling the occurrences or abundances of many species simultaneously while incorporating environmental covariates, species traits, phylogeny and spatial or temporal structure.

This makes JSDMs particularly valuable for ecologists interested in questions extending beyond the distribution of an individual species?for example, how entire communities respond to environmental gradients, which traits influence species' responses, how communities are assembled, and whether species show patterns of co-occurrence after accounting for their environmental responses. The course provides the practical R skills needed to build, assess, interpret and report these models using real ecological data.
